PAPER: JHSMR Original Article Journal of Health Science and Medical Research In Vitro Study of the Effects of Postbiotic Mouthwash Prototype with Cannabis Extracts on the Reduction of Inflammatory Cytokine: Tumor Necrosis Factor Alpha Nattapon Nisapar, DDS, MS1, Malai Taweechotipatr, Ph.D.2, Sorasun Rungsiyanont, DDS, Ph.D.1 1Department of Oral Surgery and Oral Medicine, Faculty of Dentistry, Srinakharinwirot University, Bangkok 10110, Thailand. 2Department of Microbiology, Faculty of Medicine, Srinakharinwirot University, Bangkok 10110, Thailand. Received 30 September 2024 l Revised 27 January 2025 l Accepted 17 February 2025 l Published online 11 June 2025 Abstract: Objective: This study evaluated the effects of postbiotic mouthwash containing cannabis extracts (CBD) on the reduction of tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) levels in vitro. Material and Methods: Seven mouthwash formulations were prepared using CBD at concentrations ranging from 0.25% to 1.0% v/v. TNF-α reduction was assessed using a lipopolysaccharide (LPS) model to activate the THP-1 human monocytic cell line (ATCC, TIB202). The enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) technique was employed to quantify TNF-α. Results: All formulations reduced TNF-α levels compared to the control. The most effective formulations (Preparations 1–4) achieved approximately 91% inhibition. Formulations 5–7 showed inhibition levels of 49.3%, 80.9%, and 82.5%, respectively. Conclusion: The postbiotic mouthwash containing CBD effectively reduced TNF-α levels, indicating its potential for clinical application in inflammation management. JSON: Name: postbiotic_cbd_mouthwash_tnf_reduction Title: In vitro evaluation of Lactobacillus paracasei MSMC39-1 postbiotic and cannabidiol-containing mouthwash formulations for reducing LPS-induced TNF-α secretion in THP-1 cells Short Hypothesis: Mouthwash formulations containing 10% Lactobacillus paracasei MSMC39-1 cell-free supernatant combined with 0.25–1.0% cannabidiol reduce LPS-induced TNF-α secretion from THP-1 cells more than 10% postbiotic alone in a concentration-dependent manner while maintaining cell viability above 80%. Related Work: Postbiotic preparations from Lactobacillus strains have been reported to decrease proinflammatory cytokine release in cell-based and animal models; Lactobacillus paracasei strains specifically have been associated with TNF-α attenuation. Cannabidiol (CBD) exhibits antibacterial properties and can attenuate NF-κB signaling in macrophage-line models. Existing approaches typically test single agents (postbiotic or CBD) separately or assess antimicrobial activity of cannabinoids; few studies have evaluated combined formulations or the influence of common mouthwash excipients on anti-inflammatory activity. Reported limitations include lack of systematic dose-response and cytotoxicity profiling, limited mechanistic interrogation (NF-κB pathway and TLR involvement), potential assay interference from complex formulation matrices, and scarce comparative benchmarking against clinical mouthwashes. Prior work frequently lacks standardized replication, ablation of formulation components, and concurrent antimicrobial and immunomodulatory readouts. Abstract: Postoperative oral inflammation impairs healing and is associated with elevated TNF-α. We present a structured in vitro research pipeline to evaluate mouthwash prototypes combining Lactobacillus paracasei MSMC39-1 cell-free supernatant (postbiotic) with cannabidiol (CBD) for reduction of LPS-induced TNF-α secretion from human monocytic cells. The pipeline defines standardized formulation sets, concentration ranges, cellular and microbial assays, and mechanistic endpoints to quantify anti-inflammatory efficacy, cytotoxicity, antimicrobial performance, and NF-κB pathway modulation. Main contributions are (1) a reproducible assay matrix comparing combined formulations, single-component controls, and clinical mouthwash benchmarks, (2) an ablation study of excipient and active contributions, and (3) prespecified quantitative decision criteria for selecting candidate formulations for preclinical testing. Expected outcomes are identification of one or more non-cytotoxic formulations that significantly lower TNF-α and modulate NF-κB activity in vitro while retaining antibacterial activity, providing actionable criteria for in vivo validation and clinical translation. Experiments: Cell models and reagents: THP-1 human monocytic cell line (ATCC TIB-202); LPS (E. coli O127:B8) for stimulation; mouthwash formulations: seven prototype formulations matching reported compositions (postbiotic fixed at 10% v/v; CBD at 0%, 0.25%, 0.5%, 1.0%); excipient-only base; CBD-only controls; 0.12% chlorhexidine mouthwash as clinical benchmark; saline negative control. Biological replicates: three independent cultures (biological n=3) with three technical replicates each. Treatments: pre-equilibrate THP-1 (1x10^6 cells/ml), stimulate with LPS 100 ng/ml, co-treat with formulations for 3.5 h for cytokine assays; 24 h treatments for cytotoxicity assays. Measurements: TNF-α protein by ELISA (pg/ml); TNF mRNA by qRT-PCR (ΔΔCt); cell viability by AlamarBlue and LDH release; NF-κB activation by p65 nuclear translocation (western blot) and/or NF-κB reporter assay; antimicrobial assays: planktonic CFU reduction and standardized biofilm disruption against Streptococcus mutans (gram-positive) and Escherichia coli (gram-negative); endotoxin assay and formulation interference controls. Baselines: positive control = 10% postbiotic alone; negative = saline; clinical baseline = 0.12% chlorhexidine. Ablation/Comparisons: (A) postbiotic-only vs CBD-only vs combined; (B) mouthwash base + postbiotic vs base + CBD; (C) excipient ablation: remove glycerin, polysorbate 80, saccharin individually to assess effect on TNF-α and viability; (D) CBD dose-response (0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0%); (E) fresh vs frozen postbiotic. Evaluation metrics and analysis: primary endpoint = TNF-α reduction (absolute pg/ml and percent vs saline); secondary endpoints = cell viability (%), NF-κB nuclear p65 ratio, TNF mRNA fold-change, log10 CFU reduction, biofilm biomass reduction (crystal violet OD). Statistical plan: one-way ANOVA across treatments with Tukey post-hoc for multiple comparisons; paired t-tests for matched comparisons where applicable; significance threshold p<0.05. Success criteria: ≥50% TNF-α reduction relative to saline and statistically superior to postbiotic-alone with viability ≥80%. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Biological variability of postbiotic material: strain-specific secretome composition and batch-to-batch variability may cause inconsistent activity. 2) Matrix and assay interference: formulation excipients and CBD solvents may interfere with ELISA, colorimetric viability assays, and protein assays leading to false readouts. 3) Cytotoxicity: CBD or excipient concentrations that reduce cytokines may concurrently cause cell death, confounding anti-inflammatory readouts. 4) Model limitations: THP-1 LPS-stimulated monocytic cells are a reductionist model and may not represent complex oral mucosal or tissue immune responses; results may not generalize to primary human cells or in vivo tissue. 5) Antimicrobial generalization: in vitro planktonic and biofilm assays against a limited panel do not capture polymicrobial oral ecology and may overestimate efficacy. 6) Solubility and stability: CBD solubility in aqueous mouthwash matrices and long-term formulation stability are potential technical constraints. 7) Regulatory and sourcing constraints: legal/regulatory restrictions on CBD procurement and variability in extract purity limit reproducibility. 8) Statistical power and reproducibility: modest replicate numbers can miss small effects; multiple comparisons increase false discovery risk. 9) Translatability: reduction in TNF-α in vitro does not guarantee clinical benefit for wound healing or inflammation control in humans.
